headline: DoNotNotify app offers granular control over messy Android notifications
summary: Tired of notification chaos? This free, open-source app lets you filter and manage alerts with custom rules, putting you back in control of your Android device.
details: Android notifications can be a persistent source of frustration, with many users experiencing issues like missing alerts or an overwhelming flood of spam. Even newer features like 'Cooldown' in Android 17 haven't fully resolved the problem, leaving many seeking more robust solutions.

The DoNotNotify app emerges as a powerful, free, and open-source solution for managing Android notifications. It functions as a regex-based filtering engine, allowing users to define custom rules that monitor incoming alerts and apply specific actions, such as allowing, blocking, or stacking them.

While the initial setup might seem complex, DoNotNotify is surprisingly user-friendly. It empowers users with granular control over their notification settings, a level of customization often lacking in Android's native options. The app requires notification access, permission for stacked notifications, and disabling battery optimization to function fully.

Upon installation, DoNotNotify immediately scans the device and can automatically add blocker rules for various apps, including social media and streaming services. Users are advised to review these pre-built rules carefully to avoid accidentally blocking important alerts.

The app features three main tabs: History, Rules, and Blocked. The History tab logs every notification received, organized by app, and allows users to create new rules based on specific notifications they wish to manage. This makes it easy to tailor the filtering to individual preferences.

Users can create custom rules from scratch in the Rules tab. This involves selecting an app, choosing a rule type (e.g., Title Filter, Text Filter), and configuring the filters using either simple 'Contains' toggles or more advanced 'Regex' patterns for case-insensitive and wildcard matching.

For instance, a user can set up a rule to block generic 'Congratulations' messages from a specific person on X (formerly Twitter) by using regex patterns like '(?i).*Jane Doe.*' in the Title Filter and '(?i).*congratulations.*' in the Text Filter. This ensures important messages are seen while filtering out noise.

The flexibility of DoNotNotify extends to managing time-sensitive alerts, such as real estate listings. By using the 'Contains' toggle with the agent's name in the Title Filter, users can receive all other alerts from the app while specifically filtering out rental postings.

DoNotNotify's open-source nature addresses privacy concerns, as users can inspect the code to understand exactly how their data is being handled. This transparency is a significant advantage over relying on Google's built-in, data-collecting notification management systems.

headline_marked: AI Agents [[Leak Sensitive Data]] Due to Shared File System Access
headline: AI Agents Leak Sensitive Data Due to Shared File System Access
summary: A demonstration shows how two AI agents sharing a compute instance can inadvertently expose each other's private data, highlighting a critical security flaw.
details: A recent report detailed how a Grok Bot agent, intended for posting Slack updates, mistakenly posted its CEO's bank account balances to the company's Slack channel. This occurred because the finance assistant agent and the Slack posting agent shared the same compute instance, allowing the latter to access data it was never intended to see.

Researchers reproduced this vulnerability using simple Docker Compose files, demonstrating that the issue lies not in the AI's code or prompts, but in the infrastructure's failure to provide proper isolation between agents. By mounting the same shared volume into both agents' file systems, sensitive data became accessible.

The vulnerability was fixed by simply giving each agent its own isolated volume at the shared path. This change, made outside of the agents' code and without altering their tasks, prevented the Slack agent from finding any data to leak, proving the critical importance of infrastructure-level security boundaries.

This incident underscores a common failure mode where different AI agents operating within the same environment can access each other's data if not properly sandboxed. The fix is an infrastructure decision, not a matter of agent programming or prompt engineering.

The Kubernetes agent ecosystem is actively working to standardize solutions for this shared sandbox failure mode. This issue is distinct from credential injection or network egress controls, focusing specifically on the data an agent can access on its local filesystem.
